---
name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a complete example following all
constraints below.

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

**Minimal equivalent rewrites** are allowed when Verus genuinely cannot express
a construct. The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory. Check `std_specs/`, recent additions.
3. **Minimal equivalent rewrite** — rewrite the smallest possible expression
   to an equivalent one Verus accepts. Requirements:
   - Same semantics (identical observable behavior for all inputs)
   - Same panic/error behavior
   - Same asymptotic time and space complexity
   - Smallest possible diff
   - `// VERUS REWRITE: <reason>` comment on the changed code
   - Minimal reproducer proving the original is unsupported
4. **Stdlib wrapper** — if a stdlib/core function call fails because Verus
   cannot handle the parameter types (e.g., `&mut [T]` from `DerefMut`
   coercion, closures), create a thin wrapper function whose body contains
   **ONLY** the stdlib call. Mark the wrapper `external_body` with pre/post
   conditions. The original function calls the wrapper instead. This isolates
   the trust boundary to the thinnest possible layer.

   Example — `core::mem::replace` on `&mut Vec<T>[index]`:
   ```rust
   #[verus_verify(external_body)]
   #[verus_spec(prev =>
       requires index < old(v)@.len(),
       ensures
           prev == old(v)@[index as int],
           v@ == old(v)@.update(index as int, value),
           v@.len() == old(v)@.len(),
   )]
   fn vec_replace<T>(v: &mut Vec<T>, index: usize, value: T) -> T {
       ::core::mem::replace(&mut v[index], value)
   }
   ```
   The wrapper body is a single stdlib call. The `external_body` trusts only
   this one line. The calling function remains fully body-verified.

5. **`external_body` on the original** — absolute last resort. Requires a
   minimal reproducer and `trust.md` entry.

**Principle:** prefer rewriting code to a semantic equivalent over ANY cheating.
A rewrite that lets Verus verify the body is always better than `external_body`.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition.
- **Constants**: if the initializer uses only literals and Verus-visible
  symbols, Verus sees it directly — no duplication needed. If it references
  external symbols Verus cannot resolve (e.g. `mem::PAGE_SIZE`), add a
  spec duplicate inside `verus! {}` under `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]` with
  the literal value — but keep the original **ungated** so exec code still
  uses it. Never `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies. For unavoidable ones, you must
confirm: (1) the code still builds with `cargo build`, (2) semantic code logic
is unchanged, (3) it is a genuine Verus limitation, and (4) it is documented
in `trust.md`.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Banned — only as placeholder in specification phase (must be eliminated in proving) |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's functions**: forbidden — use `admit()` instead. **On dependency functions**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified. See `crate-analysis` skill for the top-down workflow |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — do not use to "fix" verification errors |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |

---

# Spec Design Guide

## Part 1: Spec Quality Principles

### Qualities of a Good Spec

1. **Bound to exec code** — every property must appear as `requires`,
   `ensures`, or loop `invariant` on an exec function. Standalone spec
   functions that no exec function references prove nothing.
2. **Annotates the original** — specs are added directly to the original
   exec function using `#[verus_spec]` (see `verus-syntax` skill). Never
   copy exec functions into a `verus!{}` block and spec the copy — that
   verifies the copy, not the real code.
3. **Sufficient to reject bugs** — if you can imagine a buggy implementation
   that still satisfies the spec, the spec is incomplete. A sorting spec
   that omits `is_sorted` passes a function that just copies the input.
4. **Declarative, not operational** — a spec describes **what** must be true,
   not **how** the code achieves it. If you could swap quicksort for
   bubblesort and the spec still makes sense, it's a good spec.
5. **Simpler than the code** — where the code has loops, the spec has `forall`;
   where the code has bit manipulation, the spec has `Set::contains`.
6. **Independent from the code** — two independent statements of the same truth.
   If derived by reading code line-by-line, it will reproduce bugs. A useful
   test: **could you have written this spec from just the function signature,
   type definitions, and module purpose — without reading the implementation?**
   If not, the spec likely mirrors the code rather than abstracting over it.
7. **Uses mathematical objects where they simplify reasoning** — prefer `int`
   over `u32`/`i32` (avoids overflow in specs), `Seq`/`Set`/`Map` over
   `Vec`/`HashMap`. Use `view()` / `self@` for abstract state. For pointer
   addresses, prefer `usize` over `int` — addresses are inherently
   non-negative and bounded by the address space.
8. **Written for the caller** — for each ensures clause, simulate
   writing a caller's proof that uses this function. Would you use
   this fact as-is, or would you need to transform, combine, or
   unwrap it first? A good ensures clause is one the caller writes
   directly into their proof. Prefer vstd's existing spec functions
   (e.g., `self@.contains(x)`) over manual encodings (e.g.,
   `exists|i| ... && self@[i] == x`) — callers already reason with
   vstd APIs. On `exists`: valid when it genuinely hides
   implementation choice, but if the witness is computable from inputs
   and return values through the module's public spec interface,
   `exists` hides nothing — prefer a deterministic `let` binding.

### Exec Binding Rules — Desk Reject Criteria

If exec functions have no `requires`/`ensures`, the result is a **desk reject**:
nothing was verified, regardless of how many spec functions or lemmas exist in
spec.rs/proof.rs. Our goal is a **verified implementation**, not a verified
design model.

1. **Every exec function in scope gets contracts** — "in scope" is determined
   by the verification task (e.g., caller analysis, human directive, or
   module-level verification). If scope is unclear, default to all public
   and safety-critical functions. No annotation is a desk reject; partial
   annotation beats no annotation.
2. **Search vstd before writing `assume_specification`** — vstd already
   provides specs for many std library functions. Only write
   `assume_specification` for std library or third-party dependency
   functions that vstd does not cover. Never for workspace-internal code.
   Always search vstd first.
3. **Reuse dependency specs** — before calling a function from another
   module in the project, search for its `.spec.rs`:
   `find . -name "*.spec.rs" | head -20`. If the dependency has verified
   specs, import and use them directly. If it does not, add `#[verus_spec]`
   annotations on the dependency function — do NOT use `assume_specification`

   functions in module M. Specs on functions in other modules are treated as
   trusted contracts — their bodies are not checked. When those modules are
   verified later, the specs become fully proven.

2. **Use mathematical objects** — Seq, Map, Set, int/nat, not arrays/hashtables/bounded ints
3. **Abstraction should be lossy on purpose** — if spec is as complex as impl, you have no abstraction
4. **Explicit trust boundaries** — decide what is external vs external_body vs fully verified
5. **Monotonic refinement** — each layer adds detail, never changes fundamental abstraction
6. **View consistency** — if x.view() == y.view(), operations must be equivalent
7. **Spec should be obviously correct** — if spec needs a proof to understand, it's bad
8. **Specify what client needs, nothing more** — over-spec limits implementations, under-spec blocks clients

1. **Over-Faithful Abstraction** — ghost struct mirrors exec struct field-by-field → ask "what does client need?"
2. **Under-specified View** — constantly adding spec fns to expose more details → analyze client needs upfront
3. **Abstraction Leak** — spec mentions capacity, hash fn, pointers → spec must only reference View types
4. **Missing Well-formedness** — no wf() predicate → requires clauses repeat conditions everywhere
5. **Monolithic Refinement** — one-step proof from spec to impl → use intermediate layers (3 > 2)
6. **Non-Compositional Invariant** — global invariants break modularity → use local invariants + interface specs

`requires` clause here would be unsound or unusable.

**Guideline**: When both `requires` and a runtime check coexist, the
runtime check is a temporary safety net. Mark it as removable (e.g.,
`// TODO: remove once all callers are verified`) so that future
verification work knows to clean it up.

### Post-Generation Spec Refinement

After writing ensures clauses, review each one through the caller's eyes.
The guiding question: **could a caller who has never seen the implementation
find every ensures clause natural and directly useful?**

1. **Substitution test** — would this clause survive a reimplementation
   that preserves abstract behavior but changes internal strategy? If not,
   it encodes implementation detail and should be rewritten or removed.
2. **Minimality** — does this clause add information beyond what the other
   clauses already imply? Remove anything derivable from the rest.
3. **Direct usability** — can the caller use this clause as-is in their
   proof, or must they transform it first? If the latter, provide the
   form the caller actually needs.

---

## Part 2: Spec Classification

Specifications fall into three categories with different ownership:

### Internal

Specs that exist solely to help the verifier: helper lemmas, loop
invariants, intermediate assertions, proof-function pre/postconditions.
**The AI generates these freely during proving.** The test for
correctness is whether the code above can use them — the verifier
provides direct feedback.

### External-top (API contracts)

Public function `requires`/`ensures`, type invariants exposed to
callers, View types. These define **what the module promises**.
A human must review them for correctness and completeness.
Understandability is critical — a human auditor who cannot understand
the spec cannot approve it.

### External-bottom (trust assumptions)

Assumptions about layers below the verification scope: std library
behavior, hardware semantics, runtime correctness, compiler fidelity.
These are unverified: if they do not match reality, downstream proofs
may be unsound. Mechanisms include `assume_specification`,
`external_body`, and `axiom`.

### Rules

- The caller analysis and View design identify external-top properties and
  trust boundary requirements.
- When writing `assume_specification`, follow the audit checklist in
  Part 1 (Anti-Patterns, Verification Escape).
- Only genuine trust boundaries (hardware, OS, FFI, std internals) go in
  `trust.md`. Proof failures that are not trust boundaries go in
  `verification-todo.md` — see `verus-constraints` skill.

---

## Part 3: View Abstraction Design

The View type and a skeletal `inv()` should already be designed before writing
specifications. Refine and extend `inv()` as you write specs — new constraints
often emerge from requires/ensures. This section summarizes the key principles
for reference.

See `docs/specifying-and-proving-types.md` for the complete step-by-step guide
on View design, invariants, and method specifications.

1. **Only caller-visible state** — hide internal bookkeeping. Test: if you
   swapped the underlying data structure, would the View fields still make sense?
2. **Use abstract types** — `int` instead of `i32`, `Seq<int>` instead of
   `Vec<u64>`, `Map<K, V>` instead of `HashMap<K, V>`.
3. **`view()` is `pub closed spec fn`** — public so callers can invoke it,
   closed so implementation details don't leak.
4. **`inv()` is `pub open spec fn`** — includes `internal_inv()` plus
   abstraction-level properties (e.g., `self@.len() < usize::MAX`).
5. **No extra pub spec fns on `impl MyType`** beyond `inv` and `view`.
   Put reusable spec helpers on the View type instead.

For full View design methodology, see the **view-design** skill.

### Spec Transition Functions

For each state-mutating exec function, define a corresponding spec function
on the View type. Use `..self` to implicitly preserve unchanged fields
(frame condition):

```rust
impl FooView {
    pub open spec fn spec_insert(self, elem: int) -> FooView {
        FooView { elements: self.elements.insert(elem), ..self }
    }
}
// ensures self@ == old(self)@.spec_insert(elem as int)
```

**Do NOT** also list individual field changes as separate ensures — the
spec transition already captures the complete state change.

When modifying a collection element without a spec transition, state the
frame explicitly:
`forall|i: int| i != changed_idx ==> new@[i] == old@[i]`

---

## Part 4: Verus Limitations Reference

### False Limitations (AI often thinks these are blockers, but they aren't)

| "Limitation" AI claims | Reality |
|---|---|
| "Can't verify generic types" | Verus has full generic support with type bounds |
| "Can't handle &mut parameters" | &mut params are fine; only *returning* &mut is blocked |
| "Can't use closures" | FnOnce/Fn closures work; only &mut capture is blocked |
| "Need external_body for Vec/HashMap" | vstd provides full spec for Vec, HashMap, String etc. |
| "Can't do recursive specs" | Recursive spec fns work with `decreases` clause |
| "Can't verify array indexing" | `arr[i]` with bounds proof works fine |
| "Drop can't be implemented" | Drop works in verus! with `opens_invariants none no_unwind` |

### True Blockers (genuinely prevent specification)

| Blocker | Impact | Workaround |
|---|---|---|
| async/await | Cannot verify async code | `#[verifier::external]` |
| Iterator chains (.filter/.map/.collect) | No spec for combinators | Explicit loops with invariants |
| Function pointers `fn(T)->U` | Cannot pass as values | Use closures or generic bounds |
| Returning `&mut T` | Cannot write helpers returning &mut | Inline the operation |
| dyn Trait | No vtable spec | Generic dispatch or enum |
| Raw pointer deref | No direct deref | Use vstd PPtr/raw_ptr |
| Cell/RefCell | No spec | Use vstd PCell |

### Abstraction Design: Quick Reference

| Scenario | Recommended Pattern |
|---|---|
| Container/collection | Collection Lifting (Vec→Seq, HashMap→Map) + wf() |
| Nested containers | DeepView (recursive view unwrapping) |
| Smart pointer wrapping | Transparent Wrapper (Box/Rc/Arc → inner type) |
| Internal mutability | Permission Token (vstd PCell) |
| Pointer/memory ops | PointsTo + Logical ID |
| Concurrent data structure | Tokenized State Machine + Invariant |
| Complex exec struct | Ghost Struct View + wf() predicate |
| System boundary/IO | Trusted Shim (external_body + hand-written spec) |

### 8 Fundamental Abstraction Principles

1. **The abstraction gap IS the spec** — choosing the right abstraction is the core activity
2. **Use mathematical objects** — Seq, Map, Set, int/nat, not arrays/hashtables/bounded ints
3. **Abstraction should be lossy on purpose** — if spec is as complex as impl, you have no abstraction
4. **Explicit trust boundaries** — decide what is external vs external_body vs fully verified
5. **Monotonic refinement** — each layer adds detail, never changes fundamental abstraction
6. **View consistency** — if x.view() == y.view(), operations must be equivalent
7. **Spec should be obviously correct** — if spec needs a proof to understand, it's bad
8. **Specify what client needs, nothing more** — over-spec limits implementations, under-spec blocks clients

### 6 Abstraction Anti-Patterns

1. **Over-Faithful Abstraction** — ghost struct mirrors exec struct field-by-field → ask "what does client need?"
2. **Under-specified View** — constantly adding spec fns to expose more details → analyze client needs upfront
3. **Abstraction Leak** — spec mentions capacity, hash fn, pointers → spec must only reference View types
4. **Missing Well-formedness** — no wf() predicate → requires clauses repeat conditions everywhere
5. **Monolithic Refinement** — one-step proof from spec to impl → use intermediate layers (3 > 2)
6. **Non-Compositional Invariant** — global invariants break modularity → use local invariants + interface specs

# Verification Order

## Purpose

When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:
verify callees before callers. This avoids wasting effort on callers whose
callees don't yet have specs, and ensures each function's dependencies are
already proven when you reach it.

## How to Get the Order

A pre-generated verification plan may exist at:

```
{logs_dir}/verification-plan.json
```

If this file exists, use `show_fn_order.py` to display the function order:

```bash
# Show function order for a specific module
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "kernel::mm::phys::kpool"

# Glob pattern to match multiple modules
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "bitmap::*"
```

If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).

## How to Use the Order

1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.
2. **Verify functions in the listed order** (top to bottom = leaves first).
   The first function has no intra-module dependencies; later functions
   may call earlier ones.
3. **Do not skip ahead.** Resolve each function's `admit()` before moving
   to the next. This mirrors the proving-guide's "one function at a time"
   rule but with a concrete ordering.
4. **Cross-module deps** listed in the output tell you which dependency
   modules need specs. If a callee in another module lacks a spec, write
   an `assume_specification` or verify that module first.

## Output Format

```
## kernel::mm::phys::kpool
   crate: kernel  |  file: src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kpool.rs

    #  Function                        Line  In-module deps
  ───  ──────────────────────────────  ─────  ──────────────────────────────
    1  KpoolInner::alloc               L56   —
    2  KernelFrame::deref_mut          L160  —
    3  KernelFrame::clear              L144  KernelFrame::deref_mut
    4  Kpool::alloc                    L205  KpoolInner::alloc, clear
```

Use `-v` to also see cross-module dependency modules.

Functions are ordered so that by the time you reach function N, all its
intra-module dependencies (functions 1..N-1) are already verified.

name: verus-syntax
description: "Verus attribute-based syntax reference for exec functions. Covers #[verus_spec], #[verus_verify], proof!{}, proof_decl!{}, loop invariants. See GUIDE.md for advanced patterns, syntax_attr.rs for the official example."
---

# Verus Attribute-Based Syntax — Quick Reference

Use `#[verus_spec]` for exec functions, `verus! {}` for spec/proof functions.

Files in this directory:
- **SKILL.md** — this file, daily-use quick reference
- **GUIDE.md** — advanced patterns (ghost/tracked passing, dual_spec, closures, traits)
- **syntax_attr.rs** — official Verus example (from `verus-lang/verus/examples/syntax_attr.rs`)

## When to Use What

| Context | Syntax |
|---|---|
| Exec function specs | `#[verus_spec(...)]` |
| Mark external_body | `#[verus_verify(external_body)]` |
| Loop invariants | `#[verus_spec(invariant ...)]` on loop |
| Proof blocks inside exec | `proof! { ... }` |
| Function-scoped ghost vars | `proof_decl! { ... }` |
| Spec fn / proof fn | `verus! { ... }` (unchanged) |

For advanced patterns (ghost/tracked passing, dual_spec, closures, traits),
see `GUIDE.md` in this skill directory.

## #[verus_spec] — Function Specifications

```rust
#[verus_spec(sum =>
    requires
        x < 100,
        y < 100,
    ensures
        sum < 200,
)]
fn my_exec_fun(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 {
    x + y
}
```

Named return (`sum =>`) binds the return value. Omit if not needed:

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    requires x < 100,
)]
fn do_something(x: u32) { /* ... */ }
```

Bare `#[verus_spec]` marks for verification with no specs:

```rust
#[verus_spec]
fn simple_function() { /* verified, no contracts */ }
```

Supported clauses: `requires`, `ensures`, `decreases`, `returns`, `with`.

## #[verus_verify] — Verification Hints

```rust
#[verus_verify]                    // mark for verification
#[verus_verify(external_body)]     // skip body verification
#[verus_verify(external)]          // skip entirely
#[verus_verify(rlimit(50))]        // resource limit
```

Combine with `#[verus_spec]`:

```rust
#[verus_verify(external_body)]
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x > 0,
    ensures ret == x,
)]
fn wrapper(x: u32) -> u32 { x }
```

## Loop Invariants

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant
        v@ =~= Seq::new(i as nat, |k| k as u32),
)]
for i in 0..n {
    v.push(i);
}
```

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant i <= 10,
)]
while i < 10 {
    i = i + 1;
}
```

```rust
#[verus_spec(
    invariant i <= 10,
    invariant_except_break i <= 9,
    ensures i == 10, ret == 10,
)]
loop {
    i = i + 1;
    if i == 10 { ret = i; break; }
}
```

## proof! { } — Proof Blocks

Block-scoped proof code inside exec functions:

```rust
#[verus_spec(requires x < 100, y < 100)]
fn test(x: u32, y: u32) {
    proof! {
        let u = my_spec_fun(x as int, y as int);
        my_proof_fun(u / 2, y as int);
        assert(f1(3) > 3) by { reveal(f1); };
        assert(x ^ x == 0u32) by (bit_vector);
    }
}
```

## proof_decl! { } — Function-Scoped Ghost Variables

Variables persist across the entire function (not just one block):

```rust
#[verus_spec]
fn test() {
    proof_decl! {
        let ghost mut x;
        let tracked y = false;
        x = 2int;
    }
    some_exec_call();
    proof! {
        assert(x == 2);  // still in scope
        assert(!y);
    }
}
```

Only `ghost` and `tracked` declarations allowed — no exec `let`, no exec calls.

## Spec/Proof Functions (verus! { })

```rust
verus! {

pub open spec fn is_valid(x: int) -> bool {
    x >= 0 && x < 100
}

proof fn lemma_validity(x: int)
    requires is_valid(x),
    ensures x + 1 < 101,
{}

} // verus!
```

1. # Verus Attribute Syntax — Advanced Guide
2. 
3. Companion to `SKILL.md`. Covers patterns needed less frequently.
4. See also `syntax_attr.rs` in this directory for the official Verus example.
5. 
6. ---
7. 
8. ## Ghost/Tracked Parameters (`with` clause)
9. 
10. Functions can accept ghost/tracked parameters invisible to non-Verus callers.
11. 
12. ### Declaring a function with ghost/tracked params
13. 
14. ```rust
15. #[verus_spec(ret =>
16.     with
17.         Tracked(y): Tracked<&mut u32>,
18.         Ghost(w): Ghost<u64>
19.             -> z: Ghost<u32>
20.     requires
21.         x < 100,
22.         *old(y) < 100,
23.     ensures
24.         *y == x,
25.         ret == x,
26.         z == x,
27. )]
28. fn test_mut_tracked(x: u32) -> u32 {
29.     proof!{ *y = x; }
30.     #[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]
31.     x
32. }
33. ```
34. 
35. - The `with` clause declares ghost/tracked inputs and ghost outputs (`-> z: Ghost<u32>`).
36. - `#[verus_spec(with |= Ghost(x))]` on the return expression returns a ghost output.
37. 
38. ### Calling with ghost/tracked
39. 
40. Use `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` on the call expression:
41. 
42. ```rust
43. fn test_cal_mut_tracked(x: u32) {
44.     proof_decl!{
45.         let ghost mut z;
46.         let tracked mut y = 0u32;
47.         z = 0u32;
48.     }
49. 
50.     // On a let statement:
51.     #[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0) => Ghost(z))]
52.     let _ = test_mut_tracked(0u32);
53. 
54.     // On a bare expression (wrap in parens):
55.     (#[verus_spec(with Tracked(&mut y), Ghost(0))]
56.     test_mut_tracked(0u32));
57. }
58. ```
59. 
60. ### How it works
61. 
62. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` generates **two versions** of the function:
63. - A verified version (`_VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`) with ghost/tracked parameters
64. - An unverified version (original signature) with `requires false`
65. 
66. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` at the call site calls the verified version.
67. Without it, the unverified version is called — which has `requires false`,
68. so calling from verified code without the `with` annotation will fail.
69. 
70. Unverified code can call the original version normally:
71. 
72. ```rust
73. fn external_caller(x: u32) -> u32 {
74.     test_mut_tracked(1)  // calls unverified version, no with needed
75. }
76. ```
77. 
78. ### Compatibility limitation
79. 
80. `#[verus_spec(with ...)]` call-site syntax only works with exec functions
81. verified via `#[verus_spec]`. Using it to call an exec function defined
82. inside `verus! { }` will error: `cannot find function _VERUS_VERIFIED_xxx`.
83. 
84. Workaround: create a trusted wrapper:
85. 
86. ```rust
87. #[verus_verify(external_body)]
88. #[verus_spec(v =>
89.     with Tracked(perm): Tracked<&mut PointsTo<T>>
90.     requires
91.         old(perm).ptr() == ptr,
92.         old(perm).is_init(),
93.     ensures
94.         perm.ptr() == ptr,
95.         perm.is_uninit(),
96.         v == old(perm).value(),
97. )]
98. fn ptr_mut_read<'a, T>(ptr: *const T) -> T {
99.     vstd::raw_ptr::ptr_mut_read(ptr, Tracked::assume_new())
100. }
101. ```
102. 
103. ---
104. 
105. ## Dual-Mode Functions (exec → spec)
106. 
107. Automatically generate a spec mirror of an exec function:
108. 
109. ```rust
110. #[verus_verify(dual_spec(spec_add))]
111. #[verus_spec(
112.     requires x < 100, y < 100,
113.     returns add(x, y),
114. )]
115. fn add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 {
116.     proof! { assert(true); }
117.     x + y
118. }
119. // Generates: spec fn spec_add(x: u32, y: u32) -> u32 { x + y }
120. // Proof/ghost code is stripped from the generated spec function
121. ```
122. 
123. Without a custom name, an internal name `__VERUS_SPEC_xxx` is generated.
124. The `#[when_used_as_spec]` attribute lets you use the exec name as a spec:
125. 
126. ```rust
127. #[verus_verify(dual_spec)]
128. #[verus_spec(
129.     requires x < 100,
130.     returns f2(x),
131. )]
132. pub fn f2(x: u32) -> u32 {
133.     add(x, 1)
134. }
135. // Use f2(x) directly in spec context — resolves to __VERUS_SPEC_f2(x)
136. ```
137. 
138. Works on impl methods too:
139. 
140. ```rust
141. impl S {
142.     #[verus_verify(dual_spec)]
143.     #[verus_spec(
144.         returns self.foo(x),
145.     )]
146.     fn foo(&self, x: u32) -> u32 { x }
147. }
148. ```
149. 
150. **Limitations:**
151. - Requires `#[verus_spec]` — does not work with `verus!` macro
152. - `&mut` parameters are not supported (spec functions cannot take `&mut`)
153. - Not supported on trait implementations (error: "method `spec_f` is not
154.   a member of trait")
155. 
156. ---
157. 
158. ## Trait Function Specs
159. 
160. ```rust
161. trait MyTrait {
162.     #[verus_spec(r =>
163.         requires
164.             0 <= i < 10,
165.             0 <= j < 10,
166.         ensures
167.             i <= r,
168.             j <= r,
169.     )]
170.     fn compute(&self, i: u8, j: u8) -> u8;
171. }
172. ```
173. 
174. Default trait implementations:
175. 
176. ```rust
177. #[verus_verify]
178. trait SomeTrait {
179.     #[verus_spec(ret =>
180.         requires true,
181.         ensures ret,
182.     )]
183.     fn f(&self) -> bool {
184.         true
185.     }
186. }
187. ```
188. 
189. **Limitation:** `with` (ghost/tracked parameters) is not supported on
190. trait methods — error: "`with` does not support trait".
191. 
192. ---
193. 
194. ## Closure Specs
195. 
196. ```rust
197. let f =
198.     #[verus_spec(z: u64 =>
199.         requires y == 2,
200.         ensures z == 2,
201.     )]
202.     |y: u64| { y };
203. 
204. proof! {
205.     assert(f.requires((2,)));
206.     assert(!f.ensures((2,), 3));
207. }
208. let t = f(2);
209. proof! { assert(t == 2); }
210. ```
211. 
212. **Note:** Closures must have a return type annotation or a named return
213. in the spec. A closure with no return type and no named return will error:
214. "Closure must have a return type". Use either `|y: u64| -> () { }` or
215. `#[verus_spec(ret: () => ...)]`.
216. 
217. ---
218. 
219. ## Const Functions
220. 
221. ```rust
222. #[verus_spec(ret =>
223.     ensures ret == x,
224. )]
225. pub const fn identity(x: u64) -> u64 {
226.     proof! { assert(true); }
227.     x
228. }
229. 
230. pub const X: u64 = identity(1);
231. ```
232.

235. ## Macros Inside Proof Blocks
236. 
237. Rust macros can be used inside `proof_decl!`:
238. 
239. ```rust
240. macro_rules! inline_proof {
241.     ($val:expr => $x:ident, $y:ident) => {
242.         proof_decl! {
243.             let tracked $x: int = $val;
244.             let ghost $y: int = $val;
245.             assert($x == $y);
246.         }
247.     }
248. }
249. 
250. fn test() {
251.     proof_decl! {
252.         inline_proof!(0 => x, y);
253.         assert(x == 0);
254.     }
255. }
256. ```
257.

260. ## Known Limitations Summary
261. 
262. | Feature | Status |
263. |---|---|
264. | `with` call-site + `verus!{}` fn | ✗ — wrap in attribute-style fn |
265. | `dual_spec` + `&mut` params | ✗ — spec fns cannot take `&mut` |

269. | `let ghost` in exec fn | Requires `verus!{}` block — cannot use with attributes alone |
